For every integer $k\geq1$, there exist even integers

\[

\]
has a $k$-RSB Parisi measure.
\end{theorem}

claims.label: thm:gardner-main
claims.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:gardner-main}
Let $r\geq0$, and let $\Xi$ be an admissible covariance whose Parisi
measure is $r$-RSB and nondegenerate.  Define
\[
 \mathfrak p(b)=\inf_{\mu\in\M}\Pp_{b^2\Xi}(\mu),
 \qquad
 s_\Xi=\mathfrak p(1)-\mathfrak p'(1).
\]
Then $s_\Xi>0$, and there exists $\eta \in(0,2s_\Xi)$ such that, for every
sufficiently large even integer $p$, there exists a unique critical
coefficient
\[
 \lambda_{\mathrm c,p}\in(2s_\Xi-\eta,2s_\Xi+\eta)
\]
for the family
\[
 \Xi_{p,\lambda}(q)=\Xi(q)+\lambda q^p,
 \qquad
 \lambda\in[2s_\Xi-\eta,2s_\Xi+\eta],
\]
with the following phase diagram:
\[
 \begin{cases}
 r\text{-RSB}, & \lambda\leq\lambda_{\mathrm c,p},\\
 (r+1)\text{-RSB}, & \lambda>\lambda_{\mathrm c,p}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Moreover, $\lambda_{\mathrm c,p}\rightarrow2s_\Xi$ as $p\to\infty$ through even integers.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:atomic-gradient}
Let $\Xi$ be admissible, $z\in\mathcal Z_r$, $0<m\leq1$, and $q_r<Q<1$,
and let $f$ be the first-variation function of
$\mu=m\nu_z+(1-m)\delta_Q$.  Then, with $m$ and $Q$ fixed,

 \partial_{q_i}\Pp_\Xi(\mu)=-mw_if'(q_i)\quad(1\leq i\leq r),

 \partial_{w_i}\Pp_\Xi(\mu)=m\bigl(f(q_r)-f(q_i)\bigr)\quad(0\leq i<r).
\]

$f=0$ on $\supp\nu_z$ and $f'=0$ on $\supp\nu_z\setminus\{0\}$.
\end{corollary}

claims.label: rem:entropy
claims.statement_tex:
\begin{remark}\label{rem:entropy}
The quantity $s_\Xi$ is the limit of the expected entropy per spin
of the Gibbs measure $G_N(\sigma)\propto e^{H_N(\sigma)}$.  Indeed, write
$Z_N=\sum_\sigma e^{H_N(\sigma)}$ and $\langle\cdot\rangle$ for the average
under $G_N$.  The entropy
$S_N=-\sum_\sigma G_N(\sigma)\log G_N(\sigma)$ equals
$\log Z_N-\langle H_N\rangle$, and $\mathfrak p_N'(1)=N^{-1}\E\langle
H_N\rangle$, where differentiation under $\E$ is justified because
$|\partial_b\log\sum_\sigma e^{bH_N(\sigma)}|\leq\max_\sigma|H_N(\sigma)|$,
which is integrable.  Hence $N^{-1}\E S_N=\mathfrak p_N(1)-\mathfrak p_N'(1)$.  By
convexity,
$\frac1\varepsilon(\mathfrak p_N(1)-\mathfrak p_N(1-\varepsilon))
\leq\mathfrak p_N'(1)\leq
\frac1\varepsilon(\mathfrak p_N(1+\varepsilon)-\mathfrak p_N(1))$ for
$\varepsilon>0$.  We let $N\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\to0$.  Since
$\mathfrak p$ is differentiable at $1$ (see also
\cite{Panchenko2008Differentiability}), we find that
$\mathfrak p_N'(1)\to\mathfrak p'(1)$, and hence
$N^{-1}\E S_N\to s_\Xi$.
\end{remark}

claims.label: thm:gardner
claims.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:gardner}
Let $r\geq0$, and let $\Xi$ be an admissible covariance whose Parisi measure
$\mu_*$ is $r$-RSB and nondegenerate.  Define
$\mathfrak p(b)=\inf_{\mu\in\M}\Pp_{b^2\Xi}(\mu)$,
$s_\Xi=\mathfrak p(1)-\mathfrak p'(1)$, and $\lambda_{\mathrm c}=2s_\Xi$.
There exist $\eta\in(0,\lambda_{\mathrm c})$, $a_*<1$, and $C<\infty$ such
that, for every sufficiently large even integer $p$, there exists
$\lambda_{\mathrm c,p}\in(\lambda_{\mathrm c}-\eta,\lambda_{\mathrm c}+\eta)$
with the following properties.  For
$\lambda\in[\lambda_{\mathrm c}-\eta,\lambda_{\mathrm c}+\eta]$, the
covariance $\Xi_{p,\lambda}(q)=\Xi(q)+\lambda q^p$ has a unique Parisi
measure $\mu_{p,\lambda}$, and:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item If $\lambda<\lambda_{\mathrm c,p}$, then $\mu_{p,\lambda}$ is
 $r$-RSB and nondegenerate, and $\supp\mu_{p,\lambda}\subset[0,a_*]$.

 \item If $\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm c,p}$, then $\mu_{p,\lambda}$ is
 $r$-RSB and $\supp\mu_{p,\lambda}\subset[0,a_*]$.  Its first-variation
 function is nonpositive and vanishes exactly on $\supp\mu_{p,\lambda}$ and
 at one further point $Q\in(a_*,1)$.  This point satisfies, with $m=1$,
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:gardner-location}
  C^{-1}p^{-1/2}e^{-m^2\lambda p/2}
  \leq
  1-Q
  \leq
  Cp^{-1/2}e^{-m^2\lambda p/2}.
 \end{equation}
 In particular, condition~(i) of \zcref{def:nondegenerate}
 fails, so $\mu_{p,\lambda}$ is degenerate.

 \item If $\lambda>\lambda_{\mathrm c,p}$, then
 \[
  \mu_{p,\lambda}=m\nu+(1-m)\delta_Q,
 \]
 where $m\in(0,1)$, $\nu$ is an $r$-RSB probability measure with
 $\supp\nu\subset[0,a_*]$, and $Q\in(a_*,1)$ satisfies
 \eqref{eq:gardner-location} with this value of $m$.  Thus $\mu_{p,\lambda}$ is $(r+1)$-RSB.  It
 is also nondegenerate.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, $\lambda_{\mathrm c,p}\to\lambda_{\mathrm c}$ as $p\to\infty$.
By~(i)--(iii), the Parisi measure of $\Xi_{p,\lambda}$ is $r$-RSB for
$\lambda\in[\lambda_{\mathrm c}-\eta,\lambda_{\mathrm c,p}]$ and
$(r+1)$-RSB for $\lambda\in(\lambda_{\mathrm c,p},\lambda_{\mathrm c}+\eta]$,
so $\lambda_{\mathrm c,p}$ is the unique point of
$[\lambda_{\mathrm c}-\eta,\lambda_{\mathrm c}+\eta]$ at which
the number of RSB steps changes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:gardner-asymptotics}
Let $\eta$ be as in \zcref{thm:gardner}, and recall that

$g_p$ be the function of \zcref{prop:stationary-branches}(ii), and define
\[

 \frac{g_p^m}{2g_p^\lambda},
 \qquad
 g_p^\lambda=\partial_\lambda g_p(\lambda_{\mathrm c,p},1),
 \qquad
 g_p^m=\partial_mg_p(\lambda_{\mathrm c,p},1).

 \[

 \]

 $\dd\xi_s=aw_x(s,\xi_s)\dd s+\dd B_s$ with $\xi_0=x$.  Then $\xi_V$ has

Each $\psi_m$ is one-Lipschitz with $\psi_m(0)=0$, and for every compact

$\partial_m^k\partial_x^j\psi_m$ is a finite sum of terms
$x^im^{i'}\tanh^{(n)}(mx)$ with $n\geq1$ whenever $i\geq1$; since

the functions $\partial_m^k\psi_m$ are bounded in $\|\cdot\|_3$ uniformly for
$m\in I$, and they belong to $\mathcal G$ because their fourth
$x$-derivatives are bounded.  By Taylor's theorem in $m$, applied to each
$\partial_m^k\partial_x^j\psi_m(x)$, we have
$\|\partial_m^k\psi_{m+\delta}-\partial_m^k\psi_m-\delta\partial_m^{k+1}\psi_m\|_3
\leq\delta^2\sup_{m'\in I}\|\partial_m^{k+2}\psi_{m'}\|_3$ whenever
$m,m+\delta\in I$.  Hence $m\mapsto\psi_m$ is $C^\infty$ from $I$ into

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:ift-closed}
Let $D\subset\R^d$ and $K\subset\R^n$ be the compact closures of convex
open sets, let $k\geq1$, and let $\Phi\colon D\times K\to\R^n$ be $C^k$.
Suppose that, for every $\theta\in D$, the equation $\Phi(\theta,y)=0$ has
exactly one solution $y=y(\theta)$ in $K$, that this solution lies in the
interior of $K$, and that $D_y\Phi(\theta,y(\theta))$ is invertible.  Then
$y$ is $C^k$ on $D$, and its derivatives are obtained by differentiating
the identity $\Phi(\theta,y(\theta))=0$.
\end{lemma}
